Good morning, everyone. My name is Angie Kells. I am the president of the Saskatoon abortion support network and the author of the petition, which has been signed by more than 3,200 Saskatoon residents.
I would like to thank Council for receiving our petition for hearing the voices of those people who have been impacted and for bringing this conversation forward.
So our petition relates to the distribution of pamphlets delivered to Saskatoon homes and the display of large placards in public spaces containing very graphic and disturbing images.
And claiming to be aborted fetuses and the products of abortion. The pamphlets that were distributed also contained false medical information.
People were exposed to these images without the ability to consent or to opt in.
Children reported feeling very scared having nightmares crying.
Pregnant women, people who have experienced loss, people living with PTSD have reported feeling deeply distressed and traumatized.
It's really important to note that these images and the campaign that they're associated with are part of a larger movement that represent a challenge to reproductive rights.
Abortion is a fundamental human right and must be protected. When abortion is restricted, women die.
We understand that there might be concerns relating to freedom of expression, and we agree that any bylaw which has the potential to infringe on charter rights needs to be carefully considered.
Section one of the charter does allow for reasonable limits which are justified.
As Council of DuPual mentioned, several other Canadian cities have created bylaws to address this type of material.
And language used can provide guidance in creating something that will protect Saskatoon residents while maintaining charter rights.
The Canadian code of advertising standards which applies to any public messaging including these pamphlets and placards.
That's criteria for advertising that is truthful, fair, and accurate.
This allows municipal governments to veto any messaging which would violate the code, including inaccurate, discriminatory, hateful, or demeaning messages.
Several court decisions have supported cities who have used the code in relation to restricting the public distribution or display of these graphic anti-abortion images.

The 2016 court ruling between the Canadian Center for Bioethical Reform and the City of Brand Prairie stated that the CCBR has no right to force his message on an audience incapable of declining to receive it.
The decision for a pregnant person to choose abortion is one which should be made in consultation with their medical care provider.
The provider is responsible for ensuring that the patient can provide informed consent.
This requires a doctor to fully explain a procedure or treatment.
It's risks, benefits, alternative treatments, and the risks and benefits of those.
Medical professionals are really the only ones who are equipped to provide accurate, unbiased, and fact-based information to a person considering abortion.
It is irresponsible for any person or group to attempt to influence or undermine a personal medical decision by providing information which is false, misleading, or inaccurate.
As a community, we have agreed that certain content is simply not suitable for public display.
Graphic sexual images and gruesome violence are not allowed to be displayed in public.
Movies and TV shows have ratings and content warnings.
The restriction of this content allows a person to make an informed choice and to protect themselves from harm or distress by choosing what they want to view or not view.
This also demonstrates instances in which we collectively agree that reasonable limits can be applied to freedom of expression.
So in addition to the bylaw relating to the distribution of pamphlets, we are asking Council to consider bylaw which would prohibit the public.

This report deals more generally with community benefit frameworks and provides some general information to council.
Community benefit agreements and community benefit frameworks are a complex area of regulation and can mean different things in different jurisdictions.
As outlined in the report, there appear to be two different ways they are generally implemented as a condition of a development approval or as part of a procurement of capital projects.
With respect to development approvals, attention must be made to the provincial enabling legislation.
Many in Saskatchewan, we do not believe we have the legislative authority to impose community benefits as part of the development approval process.
We also note that the city of Vancouver has recently made their program non-mandatory for developers in that city.
We assume this was done in an effort to help fast-track housing supply.
With respect to the procurement of capital projects, the report notes the variety of initiatives already underway at the city that could be categorized as community benefits.
Community benefit frameworks and other jurisdictions are often managed by specific community benefit departments with a dedicated staff.
There are also challenges because of the city's obligations under our trade treaties which is detailed in the report.
The administration's plan to approach is to continue to work on the initiative already underway at the city in this area.
